title: Test quality, security, and cost
content:
Goal A working interface is not sufficient evidence that the project succeeds. This section evaluates the complete chain from upload, indexing, retrieval, answer generation, and citations to durable data, security, failure handling, and operating cost.
1. Prepare the evaluation set Select documents representative of the demonstration. Remove sensitive data, duplicates, and obsolete versions. Record each document’s name, version, page count, language, and checksum where reproducibility matters.
Create 20–30 questions covering:
Answers stated clearly in one passage. Answers requiring two passages from the same document. Similar terms or conflicting document versions. Questions with no answer in the corpus to test abstention. Vietnamese and English questions if bilingual support is claimed. Each question needs a reference answer, source document, expected passage, and question type. Do not use a chatbot-generated answer as the ground truth.
2. Functional tests ID Scenario Expected result F01 Upload a valid PDF The file is accepted, indexing completes, and no silent error occurs F02 Upload an unsupported or damaged file The system rejects it clearly without damaging the current collection F03 Ask an answerable question The answer is relevant and its citation opens the supporting passage F04 Ask an out-of-corpus question The system indicates insufficient information instead of inventing a fact F05 Restart the container Documents, indexes, and required history remain F06 Stop and start EC2 EBS mounts, the container starts, and data is accessible F07 Back up and restore Checksum passes and the restore container answers a known question Record time, commit hash, model, document set, actual result, and evidence for every case. For a failure, identify the failing step rather than recording only “failed.”
3. RAG evaluation Score three layers for each question:
Retrieval: whether the expected passage appears in the top retrieved results. Answer: whether the answer conveys the correct meaning without contradicting the corpus. Citation: whether the cited source supports the main claim. Suggested metrics:
Retrieval accuracy = questions retrieving the correct passage / answerable questions Citation support rate = answers with supporting citations / answered questions Unsupported answer rate = asserted out-of-corpus answers / out-of-corpus questions Pilot acceptance targets:
Retrieval accuracy of at least 80%. Citation support rate of at least 90%. Out-of-corpus questions should produce an insufficient-information response; investigate every unsupported assertion. For low scores, review source quality, chunking, embeddings, top-k, and the prompt before selecting a larger model.
4. Performance and dependency-failure testing Measure question receipt, retrieval completion, first response, and completed response. For the small demo, the initial target is a median response time of 15 seconds or less.
Test one, two, and a small number of concurrent users. Monitor:
EC2 CPU, memory, and disk usage. Retrieval latency and end-to-end latency. Gemini HTTP 429, timeout, and retry counts. Indexing time by document size. Retries must be bounded and use exponential backoff with jitter. Infinite bursts increase failures and make quota usage difficult to control.
5. Security tests Search Git history, Docker image metadata, and logs for GOOGLE_API_KEY, access-key patterns, and .env contents. Confirm that S3 Block Public Access remains enabled and no object is public. Use IAM Policy Simulator or a controlled negative test to verify that the role cannot access an unrelated bucket. Confirm that SSH is restricted to the administrator IP and port 7860 is not publicly exposed. Use an invalid API key and verify a controlled error without key output in logs. Verify .env mode 600 and minimal operator access. Example checks:
cd /opt/fcaj/app stat -c '%a %U:%G %n' .env sudo docker compose ps sudo ss -lntp | grep -E ':80|:7860' 6. Cost reconciliation After the test session, compare billing data with the estimate:
Actual EC2 runtime. Lifetime of the 60 GB gp3 volume. Time with a charged public IPv4 address. S3 size, object versions, and CloudWatch logs. Alarms, custom metrics, and data transfer. Gemini or other external-API charges tracked separately. The target is t3.medium for approximately 60 hours per month, estimated at USD 11.36 including 15% contingency, with a USD 15 monthly Budget. Continuous operation is estimated at approximately USD 55.89 per month, so EC2 must be stopped when idle.
7. Acceptance record Area Result Evidence Conclusion Functionality Passed tests / total tests Screenshots, logs, test sheet Pass/Fail Retrieval Correct-passage rate 20–30 question evaluation Pass/Fail Citations Supporting-source rate Source comparison Pass/Fail Performance P50, maximum, and failures Metrics and logs Pass/Fail Durability Restart and restore Archive, checksum, test evidence Pass/Fail Security Secret scan, IAM, SG, and S3 Checklist Pass/Fail Cost Actual versus estimate Billing and Budget Pass/Fail For any critical failure, record the owner, corrective action, and retest date. Do not complete the workshop while serious data-protection or secret-management defects remain.

title: Workshop
content:
Deploying FCAJ RAG Chat on AWS Overview This workshop deploys the team’s RAG document question-answering system. The Kotaemon application is packaged with Docker, runs on Amazon EC2, persists its data on Amazon EBS, and backs up to a private Amazon S3 bucket. Amazon CloudWatch and AWS Budgets provide operational and cost visibility, while the server-side application calls the Gemini API for embeddings or answer generation according to the selected configuration.
After completing the workshop, learners will be able to:
Prepare EC2, a Security Group, an IAM Role, and EBS for a RAG application. Configure Gemini safely and run FCAJ RAG Chat with Docker. Validate document upload, indexing, retrieval, and citations. Back up and restore data with S3 and verify persistence after container restarts. Monitor the system with CloudWatch, configure cost alerts, and clean up resources correctly. This architecture is intended for an academic pilot and an internal demonstration. Before serving external users, add HTTPS, authentication, dedicated secret management, and a more highly available design.
Contents Workshop introduction and architecture Prepare the account, source code, and deployment parameters Deploy the RAG application on EC2 Prepare EC2, the Security Group, and the IAM Role Install Docker, run the application, and validate it Persistent storage, backup, and monitoring Prepare and mount EBS Create a private S3 bucket and back up data Restore data and verify durability Configure CloudWatch and AWS Budgets Test quality, security, and cost Clean up resources

title: Clean up resources
content:
Congratulations on completing the FCAJ RAG Chat workshop. Cleanup is part of the lab because a stopped EC2 instance may still leave EBS, S3, public IPv4, CloudWatch, and related charges.
1. Confirm before deletion Record:
EC2 instance ID, EBS volume ID, Security Group ID, and IAM Role. S3 bucket and backup prefix. Log Group, alarms, SNS topic, and AWS Budget. Handover evidence: demo captures, test results, archive, checksum, and restore record. Agree on one option:
Pause: stop EC2 but retain EBS and backup for a future demo. Storage and public IPv4 charges may continue. Full removal: proceed only after required data has been downloaded or moved to an approved handover location. 2. Stop the workload On EC2:
cd /opt/fcaj/app sudo docker compose down sudo env APP_PORT=8080 docker compose \ -p fcaj-restore \ -f docker-compose.yml \ -f docker-compose.restore.yml \ down 2>/dev/null || true sudo systemctl stop amazon-cloudwatch-agent Verify that no workshop container is running:
sudo docker ps --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}' 3. Remove observability resources In CloudWatch and SNS:
Delete fcaj-rag-chat alarms after saving required evidence. Delete the dedicated dashboard, if created. Delete /fcaj/rag-chat/application if logs do not require retention. Delete workshop-only SNS subscriptions and topics. Delete fcaj-rag-chat-monthly if the project no longer needs tracking. Do not delete shared topics, Log Groups, or Budgets.
4. Handle the S3 backup Verify the exact bucket and number of object versions. Retain it when handover data is required. For full removal:
Confirm that the bucket belongs to this workshop. Remove all object versions and delete markers because Versioning is enabled. Confirm that the bucket is empty. Delete the bucket. This cannot be recovered without another copy. Never use a wildcard or an unverified variable to select the bucket.
5. Remove EC2 and EBS Select fcaj-rag-chat-demo and Terminate instance for full removal. Wait for the terminated state. Under Volumes, locate the recorded Volume ID tagged fcaj-rag-chat-data. Confirm that it is available and not attached elsewhere. Delete the 60 GB volume when its data is no longer required. Release only an Elastic IP dedicated to the workshop. An automatically assigned public IPv4 is normally released on termination. 6. Remove permissions and networking After EC2 termination and when the instance profile is unused:
Detach policies from fcaj-rag-chat-ec2-role. Delete the dedicated role and instance profile. Delete the backup customer managed policy after confirming no other role uses it. Delete fcaj-rag-chat-sg after its network-interface references disappear. Do not delete a shared VPC, subnet, or IAM policy.
7. Post-cleanup cost check EC2: no running or stopped workshop instance. EBS: no volume or snapshot outside the retention list. EC2 networking: no orphaned Elastic IP or network interface. S3: the bucket is deleted or has a named owner and retention policy. CloudWatch/SNS: dedicated alarms, logs, dashboards, and topics are handled. IAM: dedicated role, instance profile, and policy are deleted. Budgets: retained only if the project continues. Billing and Cost Explorer may update with delay. Check again the next day and monitor budget email until no charge-generating resource remains.
Never delete shared data or resources because a name looks similar. Verify ID, tag, Region, and owner before every deletion.

title: Self-Assessment
content:
At the current stage of my internship in the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program, which runs from June 22, 2026, to August 15, 2026, I have had the opportunity to study and practice cloud computing, AWS services, teamwork, and the delivery process of a technical project.
Through weekly labs and worklogs, I have explored AWS CLI, Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, CloudFront, Amazon RDS, Elastic Load Balancing, Auto Scaling, CloudWatch, Route 53 Resolver, IAM, and other related services. I have also participated in studying and preparing the deployment of fcaj-rag-chat, a RAG Web Chat application based on Kotaemon, Docker, and Gemini. The project is currently being configured and tested locally in preparation for deployment with Amazon ECR, Amazon ECS Fargate, and Amazon EFS.
The program includes approximately ten in-person sessions, while most work is completed through self-study at home. This format has helped me develop the ability to research documentation independently, manage progress, record results, and communicate with mentors or team members when I encounter an issue.
To provide an objective reflection on my internship progress, I assessed myself using the following criteria:
No. Criteria Description Excellent Good Average 1 Professional knowledge and skills Understanding foundational knowledge, using tools, and applying them in labs or the project ☐ ✅ ☐ 2 Ability to learn Acquiring new knowledge and proactively researching documentation ☐ ✅ ☐ 3 Proactiveness Planning, researching, and completing work without depending entirely on instructions ✅ ☐ ☐ 4 Sense of responsibility Tracking progress, completing tasks, and recording results clearly ✅ ☐ ☐ 5 Discipline Following schedules and rules while maintaining self-study progress ✅ ☐ ☐ 6 Growth mindset Receiving feedback, recognizing limitations, and adjusting working methods ✅ ☐ ☐ 7 Communication Presenting ideas, reporting progress, and describing technical issues ☐ ✅ ☐ 8 Teamwork Coordinating, sharing information, and agreeing on responsibilities with team members ✅ ☐ ☐ 9 Professional conduct Respecting mentors, participants, and the learning environment ✅ ☐ ☐ 10 Problem-solving skills Analyzing causes, testing hypotheses, and proposing solutions ☐ ✅ ☐ 11 Contribution to the project Completing assigned work and contributing documentation, testing, and architecture ideas ✅ ☐ ☐ 12 Overall assessment Overall progress and level of completion throughout the internship ☐ ✅ ☐ Strengths Independent learning and knowledge acquisition
Because most of the program is based on self-study at home, I have practiced reading workshops and technical documentation and following instructional videos before turning what I learned into a lab or worklog entry. I can approach new groups of AWS services and gradually connect them into a more complete architecture.
Proactiveness during hands-on work
I proactively prepare the environment, follow configuration steps, validate results, and clean up resources after labs. In the project, I have studied the repository and analyzed its Dockerfile, Docker Compose configuration, Gemini settings, and persistence mechanism based on ChromaDB, LanceDB, and SQLite.
Ability to organize technical knowledge
Maintaining weekly worklogs helps me organize objectives, tasks, references, and results. I now have a clearer understanding of the relationships among compute, storage, networking, databases, security, and monitoring instead of treating each service as an isolated topic.
Collaboration and openness to feedback
During in-person sessions and project discussions, I communicate with mentors and team members to agree on an approach. I am willing to revise content or technical decisions when I receive relevant feedback.
Areas for Improvement Hands-on cloud deployment experience
I have gained a foundation through labs and architecture design, but my experience deploying a complete application on AWS remains limited. The RAG project is still running locally and being prepared for deployment, so I need additional practice with ECR, ECS Fargate, EFS, ALB, IAM, SSM Parameter Store, and CloudWatch Logs during the remaining weeks.
Systematic troubleshooting
When I encounter an issue in an unfamiliar area, I sometimes need additional time to identify its cause. I need to improve my troubleshooting sequence by checking the original requirement, configuration, credentials, IAM permissions, network path, logs, resource status, and actual result. Recording hypotheses and each validation step will help me avoid unfocused trial and error.
Time management and focus
A flexible self-study format can lead to an overly broad learning scope. I need to break work into small deliverables, assign a deadline to each part, and complete the main objective before researching additional topics.
Technical communication
I need to describe issues more clearly and concisely by including the objective, environment, reproduction steps, expected behavior, actual behavior, relevant logs, and previous attempts. This structure will allow mentors and team members to provide more effective support.
Testing and delivery quality
I need to continue improving how I design test cases, negative tests, health checks, and acceptance criteria. For the RAG project, this includes validating PDF upload, indexing, retrieval, citations, persistent data, secret management, and recovery after a container restart.
Improvement Plan Complete the project deployment and testing tasks planned for Weeks 6–8 without reporting a task as complete before evidence is available. Use a checklist for each lab and project task, including preparation, implementation, testing, evidence collection, and cleanup. Plan self-study activities by week, prioritize required deliverables, and limit time spent on out-of-scope topics. Record logs, errors, root causes, and resolutions to build reusable troubleshooting experience. Practice reporting progress and describing technical issues using a consistent structure. Continue studying AWS security, monitoring, cost optimization, and system operations. Conclusion: At the current stage, the internship has helped me establish an AWS foundation, improve my independent learning skills, and better understand the process of moving an application from a local environment to a cloud architecture. I recognize that I still need more experience in hands-on deployment, testing, and troubleshooting. Therefore, an overall rating of Good appropriately reflects both my current progress and the skills I need to continue developing during the remaining internship period.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Overall Evaluation At this stage, the First Cloud AI Journey program has given me the opportunity to approach AWS through a combination of foundational knowledge, hands-on labs, and a team project. The learning process goes beyond using individual services and helps me understand how to select, connect, and operate components within a cloud architecture.
1. Learning environment and working format
The program combines approximately ten in-person sessions with predominantly self-directed study at home. The in-person sessions are useful for discussing issues with mentors, meeting other participants, and resolving topics that are difficult to communicate through documentation alone. Self-study provides flexibility but also requires proactive planning, progress management, and independent technical research.
2. Support from mentors and program coordinators
The mentors and program coordinators provide direction, reference materials, and assistance during the learning process. I appreciate that mentors suggest an analytical approach and allow participants to experiment and identify the cause of an issue instead of only providing an answer. This approach improves both troubleshooting skills and the ability to explain technical problems.
3. Relevance of the program content
The curriculum progresses from AWS fundamentals to more systematic hands-on exercises. I have explored AWS CLI, EC2, S3, CloudFront, RDS, ALB, Auto Scaling, CloudWatch, Route 53 Resolver, IAM, and other related services. Combining these topics with a project helps turn individual concepts into practical architectural knowledge.
4. Technical skill development
The worklogs and labs have improved my ability to read documentation, configure resources, validate connectivity, inspect logs, and troubleshoot errors. Through the fcaj-rag-chat project, I have studied the Kotaemon architecture, Docker Compose, Gemini, ChromaDB, LanceDB, and SQLite while preparing a deployment plan based on Amazon ECR, Amazon ECS Fargate, and Amazon EFS. At this stage, the project is being configured and tested locally in preparation for AWS deployment.
5. Teamwork and reporting skills
Weekly worklogs help me record objectives, tasks, references, and results in a structured way. During the project, the team needs to discuss architecture, divide responsibilities, report progress, and agree on test criteria. This provides an opportunity to practice clear communication and evidence-based collaboration.
6. Program policies and participation conditions
The internship program does not provide an allowance. The combination of in-person sessions and self-study at home offers scheduling flexibility, but the outcome depends heavily on each participant’s initiative. Additional AWS sandbox access, lab credits, or detailed cost-control guidance would make it easier to practice services that may incur charges.
Additional Questions What have you found most satisfying during the program?
The most satisfying part is the progression from studying individual AWS services to analyzing a real project. Through fcaj-rag-chat, I have gained a clearer understanding of how a RAG application processes documents, creates embeddings, builds indexes, retrieves context, and generates answers with citations. Designing how to containerize the application and map its architecture to ECR, ECS Fargate, and EFS has helped me understand the relationship among the application, persistent data, and cloud infrastructure.
What could the program improve for future interns?
The program could provide a clearer weekly roadmap in which each phase has specific objectives, deliverables, and completion criteria. In addition to self-study materials, short mentor checkpoints, an architecture review before deployment, and AWS cost-management guidance would help participants avoid overly broad learning paths and identify design problems earlier.
Would you recommend the program to a friend? Why?
Yes. I would recommend the program to people who want to learn AWS through theory, labs, and a practical project. However, participants should be prepared for substantial self-study because most work is completed at home. The program is best suited to proactive learners who are willing to research documentation, record their practice, and discuss issues when they need support.
Suggestions and Expectations Suggestions for improving the program experience:
Provide a weekly roadmap, deliverable checklist, and consistent evaluation criteria from the beginning. Hold periodic checkpoints so mentors can review progress, architecture decisions, and technical issues. Add guidance on AWS Budgets, cost alerts, resource cleanup, and safe resource usage. Consider providing an AWS sandbox or lab credits for exercises that may incur charges. Organize short sharing sessions where each team can present its architecture, demonstrate results, and discuss lessons learned. Provide common templates for evidence, test cases, and incident reports to make weekly worklogs more consistent. Would you like to continue with this program in the future?
Yes. If given the opportunity, I would like to continue developing my AWS deployment, monitoring, cost-optimization, and security skills. I would also like to continue evolving the project from a local application into a system that is fully deployed and tested in a cloud environment.
Any other comments?
The program has helped me understand that learning cloud computing is not only about knowing the names of services or how to create them. It also requires attention to security, cost, operability, persistent data, and testing. Combining self-study, labs, worklogs, and a team project creates a highly practical learning path. I appreciate the guidance and opportunities for discussion that I have received and hope the program continues to strengthen its technical checkpoints so participants can turn separate pieces of knowledge into a complete and verifiable solution.
